origin.fact: Developed in Thailand by breeder Kitti Phanaitthi and introduced in the early 1990s.
Appeared in the early 1990s as a mutation in Asian discus breeding. The name comes from the 'pigeon blood' ruby colour.
Said to come from a Schmidt-Focke-line striped turquoise male crossed with a red turquoise female. Kitti showed the fish at Aquarama in 1991, and they then spread around the world.
A forum poster says the English name came later than the Thai one. Another poster calls it a marketing label for dark red.
The original Pigeon Blood form no longer exists. It has been crossed into many other discus forms.

looks.fact: Pale white-to-cream or orange-red base with red striping or marbling. Little or no dark vertical barring. Deep red eyes.
Pigeon fish do not darken or show the usual vertical bars in unfamiliar surroundings. Juveniles of 5–7 cm already show adult colour.
Black peppering (irregular black specks) was heavy in the original fish. Modern fish are judged better with little peppering, richer red and more white.
Peppering is melanin scattered as fine black dots and is tied to the pigeon mutation. Good husbandry keeps it to a minimum, but the gene cannot be removed.

lines.fact: Red Melon, Marlboro Red and Red Passion all trace back to the original Pigeon Blood.
Pigeon Blood Panda: a red-turquoise type with a red base, turquoise spots in a checkerboard pattern and partly blackish dorsal and anal fins.
There are dozens of Pigeon Blood varieties, and each farm gives its own names, so names are not standardised.

keeping.fact: Keep in groups of 4–6 in a cycled tank of at least about 190 L (50 US gal) for one fish, plus about 38 L (10 gal) for each extra fish. Plants such as Java fern, anubias and Amazon sword, plus driftwood, suit them.
Peaceful. Good tankmates are cardinal, neon and glowlight tetras, hatchetfish and sterbai corydoras.
Feed live, frozen or freeze-dried food (brine shrimp, bloodworm, daphnia) plus some vegetables. Feed adults about 3 times a day and juveniles about 5 times.

Vietnamese keepers feed minced beef heart, tubifex worms and prepared food in many small meals. They need very clean water and warn against keeping plecos with discus, because plecos suck the discus' slime coat.
Dark backgrounds can make pigeon fish develop black peppering. Bright light and pale backgrounds are suggested instead.

breeding.fact: Breeds like other discus: both parents guard the eggs, eggs hatch in about 60 hours, and fry feed on the parents' skin mucus for the first 5–6 days. Use soft, acidic water (pH 5.5–6) in a separate tank.
The strain was never stabilised, so offspring split much like the parents did (about half red turquoise and half striped turquoise in the first cross).

Pigeon parents often do not darken while breeding, so fry may struggle to find them. Hobbyists suggest white or pale blue tank walls, covering dark sponges in white nylon, and lowering the water level.
One poster says the colour form itself does not make a better or worse parent; individual fish matter more.

health.fact: The main strain-specific flaw is black peppering, which can show up with stress or dark surroundings. Otherwise the fish are described as hardy.
Peppering can come from genes, stress and surroundings.
Discus in general easily get gut disease and gill flukes, which can spread through a whole group if not treated quickly.

buying.fact: Pick fish with little peppering, clean red colour and red eyes. Good pigeon-based lines have had most of the peppering culled out.
To acclimate: keep lights off for at least 4 hours, do not feed for the first 24 hours, and drip or float to adjust the fish to the water.
In Vietnam the fish are sold as juveniles of 7–9 cm, often listed together with red discus.

controversy.fact: Hobbyists on forums say opinion changed: peppering used to be liked and is now mostly unwanted. One poster blames breeders for pushing the trait on easily swayed buyers.
A forum poster dismisses the name 'pigeon blood' as marketing for a dark red fish.
